title: DFS: Fundamentals
summary: Learn the fundamentals of Depth-First Search: how DFS traverses binary trees using recursion, the call stack, and backtracking.

sections.heading: Binary Tree Properties
sections.body:
A **binary tree** has a **root** node at the top. Each node can have at most two children: a **left child** and a **right child**. Nodes without children are **leaf nodes**.

**Height**: The number of edges on the longest path from the root to a leaf.

**Balanced**: A tree where the height of left and right subtrees of every node differ by at most 1.

**Complete**: Every level except possibly the last is completely filled, and nodes are as far left as possible. Complete trees have height O(log n).

**Binary Search Tree (BST)**: All nodes in the left subtree are less than the root; all nodes in the right subtree are greater. This property applies recursively to all subtrees.

sections.heading: Depth-First Search Algorithm
sections.body:
**Depth-First Search (DFS)** traverses every node in a binary tree by going "down" as far as possible before backtracking. It starts at the root and tries to reach a leaf node, then backtracks to explore the next path.

This "go deep then backtrack" behavior differentiates DFS from Breadth-First Search (BFS), which explores all nodes at one level before moving to the next.

sections.heading: Recursion and the Call Stack
sections.body:
DFS is typically implemented as a **recursive function** that calls itself. Understanding the **call stack** is essential.

**Call Frame**: When a function is called, a call frame is pushed onto the call stack containing the current line of execution and local variables.

**Pushing to the Stack**: Each recursive call to `dfs(node.left)` or `dfs(node.right)` pushes a new call frame onto the stack.

**Base Case**: When `node` is `None`, the function returns without making further recursive calls. This stops the traversal from going deeper.

**Backtracking**: When a function returns, its call frame is popped off the stack, and execution returns to the previous call frame. This is how DFS backtracks to explore other paths.

sections.heading: DFS Traversal Process
sections.body:
1. Start at the root node
2. Make a recursive call to the left child
3. Continue recursively until reaching a `None` node (base case)
4. Return and backtrack to the parent
5. Make a recursive call to the right child
6. Repeat until all nodes are visited

When a recursive call returns, we have finished visiting all nodes in both the left and right subtrees of the current node.

sections.heading: Complexity Analysis
sections.body:
**Time Complexity**: O(N) where N is the number of nodes. DFS visits each node exactly once. If each recursive call does constant work, the overall time is O(N).

**Space Complexity**: O(H) where H is the height of the tree. This accounts for the recursive call stack. In the worst case (unbalanced tree), H = N, so space is O(N). For a balanced tree, H = O(log N).

approach: DFS uses recursion to traverse trees by going as deep as possible before backtracking
Every recursive DFS function has a base case (typically `if not node: return`) to stop traversal
Recursive calls are made on left and right children to explore subtrees
The call stack manages the traversal and enables automatic backtracking when functions return
After a recursive call returns, all nodes in that subtree have been visited
code:
def dfs(node):
    # Base case: stop when we reach None
    if node is None:
        return
    
    # Recursive case: visit left subtree
    dfs(node.left)
    
    # Recursive case: visit right subtree
    dfs(node.right)
    
    # When we return here, all nodes in both
    # left and right subtrees have been visited

quiz.q: What happens when a DFS recursive call reaches a None node?
options: The function returns and the call frame is popped from the stack, causing backtracking
The function continues to the next node in the tree
The function starts over from the root
quiz.explain: When node is None, the base case triggers a return. This pops the current call frame off the stack and returns execution to the previous call frame, which is the backtracking mechanism in DFS.

quiz.q: What is the space complexity of DFS on a balanced binary tree with n nodes?
quiz.explain: The space complexity is determined by the maximum depth of the call stack, which equals the height of the tree. A balanced binary tree has height O(log n), so the space complexity is O(log n).
